{{short description|American virologist (1926–2020)}}
'''Harry Rubin''' (June 23, 1926<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale, 2005</ref> – February 2, 2020)<ref name=obit>{{cite news|title=Virus expert and cancer biologist Harry Rubin dies at 93|newspaper=Berkeley News|publisher=UC Berkeley|url=https://news.berkeley.edu/2020/02/07/virus-expert-and-cancer-biologist-harry-rubin-dies-at-93/|author=Sanders, Robert|date=February 7, 2020}}</ref> was an American cell biologist and virologist. He is known for his experimental research on [[oncovirus]]es and how cellular microenvironment and cellular aging affect the regulation of [[cancer]]ous tumors.<ref name=obit/><ref>{{cite web|title=Harry Rubin|website=Department of Cellular & Molecular Biology, UC Berkeley|url=http://mcb.berkeley.edu/index.php?option=com_mcbfaculty&name=rubinh|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090104203203/http://mcb.berkeley.edu/index.php?option=com_mcbfaculty&name=rubinh |archive-date=2009-01-04 }}</ref>

==Biography==
His parents were Jewish immigrants and his father had a grocery store and delicatessen in Manhattan. Harry Rubin graduated in 1947 as a Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (D.V.M.) from the [[New York State College of Veterinary Medicine at Cornell University]]. From 1947 to 1948 he served in the joint U.S.-Mexican Aftosa Commission dealing with an outbreak of [[hoof-and-mouth disease]] (''fiebre aftosa'' in Spanish) among cattle in Mexico.<ref name=Martin/><ref>{{cite journal|author=McCulloch, A. E.|title=We're Winning the Battle of Aftosa|journal=The Rotarian|volume=LXXV|issue=6|pages=26–28|date=December 1949|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r0YEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA26}}</ref> From 1948 to 1952 he was stationed in [[Montgomery, Alabama]] as a commissioned officer of the [[United States Public Health Service]]. In January 1952 he married Dorothy Margaret Shuster, who was being trained as a flight evacuation nurse in the U.S. Air Force when he met her.<ref name=Martin>{{cite web|author=Martin, G. Steven|title=In Memoriam. Harry Rubin|website=Academic Senate, University of California|year=2021|url=https://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/in-memoriam/files/harry-rubin.html}}</ref>

In 1952 he was briefly enrolled as a graduate student at [[New York University]], but [[Wendell Stanley]] recruited him to work at [[UC Berkeley]]'s Virus Laboratory. From 1952 to 1953 Rubin was a research fellow at UC Berkeley. From 1953 to 1958 he was a research fellow at [[Caltech]]. There he worked in [[Renato Dulbecco]]'s laboratory and discovered in 1955 that, in a tumor infected with [[Rous sarcoma virus]] (RSV), every cell in the tumor is capable of releasing RSV. In 1958 [[Howard Temin|Temin]] and Rubin published an important paper ''Characteristics of an assay for Rous sarcoma virus and Rous sarcoma cells in tissue culture'' on their breakthrough in developing a tissue culture assay for RSV. At UC Berkeley, Rubin was an associate professor from 1958 to 1960 and a full professor from 1960 to 2001, when he retired as professor emeritus.<ref name=Martin/>

At UC Berkeley's Virus Laboratory, Rubin, working with postdoctoral fellows, [[Peter K. Vogt]] and [[Hidesaburo Hanafusa]], demonstrated that [[avian sarcoma leukosis virus]] (ASLV) can act as a "[[helper virus]]" for RSV. This research earned Rubin the 1964 [[Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research]] (shared with [[Renato Dulbecco]]).<ref name=Martin/>

Rubin received in 1961 the [[Eli Lilly and Company-Elanco Research Award|Eli Lilly Award in Bacteriology and Immunology]] and in 1963 the Merck Research Award. He was elected in 1978 a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=Martin/>

He was "a singer and guitar player much in demand at parties."<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-QMBiN1vorsC&pg=PA540|page=540| isbn=9780299166045 | editor=Crow, James Franklin |editor2=Dove, William F. |title=Perspectives on Genetics: Anecdotal, Historical, and Critical Commentaries, 1987-1998 | year=2000 | publisher=Univ of Wisconsin Press }}</ref> During the 1960s he was active in Berkeley's anti-Vietnam war movement. In the 1970s he became interested in Jewish ethics and the ideas of some Jewish philosophers such as [[Emmanuel Levinas]], [[Franz Rosenzweig]], [[Joseph B. Soloveitchik]], and [[Eliezer Berkovits]]. Rubin and his wife joined the Congregation Beth Israel in Berkeley, and he met regularly with a philosophy discussion group of congregation members.<ref name=Martin/>

His doctoral students include [[Howard M. Temin]] and [[Gail R. Martin]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Harry Rubin, D.V.M.|website=Cell Biology Tree (academictree.org)|url=https://academictree.org/cellbio/peopleinfo.php?pid=58967}}</ref>

Harry and Dorothy Rubin had two sons and two daughters. He died on February 2, 2020.<ref name=Martin/> His grave is in Gan Shalom Cemetery, [[Contra Costa County, California]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Harry Rubin (search)|website=Gan Shalom Cemetery, Contra Costa County|url=https://www.findagrave.com/cemetery/2257372/gan-shalom-cemetery}}</ref>
